KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) -- Nepal's former king said Wednesday he is not going to leave his country even though the monarchy has been abolished. Gyanendra came to power in 2001 following the assassination of King Birendra and his family. Ex-King Gyanendra, 60, made remarks to reporters before departing the Narayanhiti royal palace in Kathmandu. He will live as a civilian in the former Himalayan kingdom that was made a republic last month, and he will reside in a summer palace on a forested hilltop outside the capital. A few hundred journalists crammed into the opulent palace's lobby entrance to hear Gyanendra's remarks. It was a chaotic and undeferential scene replete with pushing, shoving and scuffling -- even while the former monarch was speaking. While the former king spoke, reporters looked around at the lavish furnishings, including a huge crystal chandelier, stuffed tigers, stuffed rhino heads mounted on the walls and paintings of previous monarchs. Gyanendra, who expressed his "love" for "independent Nepal," said all of his property will remain in the country and that he has no property outside the nation. "I have no intention or thoughts to leave the country," he said. "I will stay in the country to help establish peace." The monarchy's end after 239 years of rule was the culmination of a two-year peace process in which Maoist insurgents in Nepal gave up their armed struggle, joined mainstream politics and won the most seats in April's election for the Constituent Assembly. The assembly is tasked with rewriting the constitution, deciding the country's future political system and governing the nation. Gyanendra, who noted that the country is going through a "serious" stage now, said he accepts the new reality of a republic and reflected on the actions of the monarchy. "I have done all I can to cooperate with (the government's) directives," he said, and added that "the monarchy in Nepal has always been with the people of Nepal in good times and bad times." Gyanendra came to power in 2001 when his brother, King Birendra, and his family were massacred in the palace by the crown prince, who later shot himself. Gyanendra on Wednesday denied rumors that he had played a role in that event. The ex-monarch also discussed events of 2005, when he he took over the civilian government to take on the Maoist insurgency, an unpopular move that sparked protests. He said he hopes people "understand" he didn't intend to infringe on any of the rights of the people. He left the palace by a side entrance with pro-royalists and pro-republicans gathered outside to see his departure. His car had to stop momentarily as journalists took pictures of him. Gyanendra's royal scepter and a crown of peacock feathers, yak hair and jewels remain in the palace and have been handed over to the government. -- From CNN's Dan Rivers and Manesh Shrestha .

Gyanendra, 60, came to power in 2001 following the assassination of King Birendra and his family. The former king made his remarks to reporters before departing the Narayanhiti royal palace in Kathmandu. He will now live as a civilian in the former Himalayan kingdom, which was declared a republic last month, and will reside in a summer palace on a forested hilltop outside the capital.

A few hundred journalists crowded into the entrance lobby of the opulent palace to hear Gyanendra speak. The scene was chaotic and notably lacking in deference, marked by pushing, shoving and scuffles — even as the former monarch delivered his remarks.

As he spoke, reporters surveyed the palace’s lavish furnishings, including a massive crystal chandelier, stuffed tigers, stuffed rhinoceros heads mounted on the walls and portraits of previous monarchs.

Gyanendra, expressing his “love” for an “independent Nepal,” said all of his property would remain in the country and that he owns no property abroad.

“I have no intention or thoughts to leave the country,” he said. “I will stay in the country to help establish peace.”

The monarchy’s end, after 239 years of rule, marked the culmination of a two-year peace process in which Nepal’s Maoist insurgents abandoned their armed struggle, entered mainstream politics and won the largest number of seats in April’s election for the Constituent Assembly.

The assembly is responsible for rewriting the constitution, determining the country’s future political system and governing the nation.

Gyanendra, noting that the country is now passing through a “serious” stage, said he accepts the new reality of a republic and reflected on the monarchy’s actions.

“I have done all I can to cooperate with [the government’s] directives,” he said, adding that “the monarchy in Nepal has always been with the people of Nepal in good times and bad times.”

Gyanendra first came to power in 2001, after his brother, King Birendra, and Birendra’s family were massacred in the palace by the crown prince, who later shot himself. On Wednesday, Gyanendra denied rumors that he had played any role in the killings.

The former monarch also addressed the events of 2005, when he took over the civilian government in an effort to confront the Maoist insurgency — an unpopular move that sparked protests. He said he hopes people “understand” that he did not intend to infringe upon any of their rights.

He left the palace through a side entrance, as both pro-royalists and pro-republicans gathered outside to witness his departure. His car briefly stopped as journalists photographed him.

Gyanendra’s royal scepter and a crown made of peacock feathers, yak hair and jewels remain in the palace and have been handed over to the government.

KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) — Nepal’s former monarch said on Wednesday that he does not plan to leave the country, despite the formal abolition of the monarchy.

Gyanendra became king in 2001 after King Birendra and members of his family were killed. The 60-year-old former king spoke to reporters before leaving the Narayanhiti royal palace in Kathmandu. He will now live as an ordinary citizen in the former Himalayan kingdom, which was declared a republic last month, and will move into a summer residence on a wooded hilltop outside the capital.

Several hundred journalists packed tightly into the entrance lobby of the ornate palace to listen to him. The atmosphere was disorderly and lacked the usual deference associated with royalty, with pushing, jostling and scuffles continuing even as the former king delivered his remarks.

As Gyanendra spoke, reporters took in the palace’s extravagant interior, which included a large crystal chandelier, stuffed tigers, mounted rhinoceros heads on the walls and portraits of earlier monarchs.

Gyanendra spoke of his “love” for “independent Nepal” and said that all of his assets would remain inside the country, adding that he owns no property abroad.

“I have no intention or thoughts to leave the country,” he said. “I will stay in the country to help establish peace.”

The end of Nepal’s 239-year-old monarchy marked the conclusion of a two-year peace process. During that period, Maoist rebels abandoned their armed campaign, entered mainstream politics and secured the largest number of seats in April’s election for the Constituent Assembly.

That assembly is responsible for drafting a new constitution, determining Nepal’s future political structure and running the country.

Gyanendra acknowledged that Nepal is currently passing through a “serious” period. He said he accepts the new republican reality and looked back on the monarchy’s role.

“I have done all I can to cooperate with [the government’s] directives,” he said, adding that “the monarchy in Nepal has always been with the people of Nepal in good times and bad times.”

Gyanendra took the throne in 2001 after his brother, King Birendra, and Birendra’s family were killed inside the palace by the crown prince, who later shot himself. On Wednesday, Gyanendra rejected allegations that he had been involved in those events.

The former king also addressed the events of 2005, when he assumed control of the civilian government in an effort to confront the Maoist rebellion. That decision was widely unpopular and led to demonstrations. He said he hoped people would “understand” that he had not meant to violate anyone’s rights.

He exited the palace through a side entrance, while both royalist supporters and republicans gathered outside to watch him leave. His vehicle briefly had to stop as journalists photographed him.

Gyanendra’s royal scepter and his crown, made with peacock feathers, yak hair and jewels, remain inside the palace and have been transferred to the government.

— From CNN’s Dan Rivers and Manesh Shrestha

“I have no intention of leaving the country,” he said in a rare news conference. “I will stay in Nepal and work for the peace and prosperity of the Nepali people.”

Gyanendra was expected to move to Nagarjun, a former royal residence on a forested hill on the outskirts of Kathmandu. Government officials said the Narayanhiti palace, long closed to ordinary Nepalis, would be converted into a national museum.

The departure marked the most visible symbol of Nepal’s transformation from the world’s only Hindu kingdom into a federal democratic republic. On May 28, the first sitting of the Constituent Assembly voted overwhelmingly to abolish the monarchy, ending a royal institution that had unified Nepal in the 18th century and dominated its politics for much of the country’s modern history.

The assembly’s decision followed a decade-long Maoist insurgency, a 2006 popular uprising against Gyanendra’s direct rule, and a peace process that brought the former rebels into mainstream politics. The Maoists emerged as the largest party in the April Constituent Assembly election, campaigning strongly for an end to the monarchy.

Gyanendra became king in 2001 after a massacre at the palace in which King Birendra, Queen Aishwarya and several other members of the royal family were killed by Crown Prince Dipendra, according to official accounts. Gyanendra’s popularity declined sharply after he dismissed the government and seized absolute power in 2005, saying he needed to defeat the Maoist rebellion and restore order.

Mass protests in April 2006 forced him to relinquish direct rule and restore parliament. The revived legislature stripped him of most powers, brought the army under civilian control, ended Nepal’s status as a Hindu kingdom and paved the way for elections to the Constituent Assembly.

Security was tight around Narayanhiti on Wednesday, though the atmosphere in the capital was largely calm. Small groups of onlookers gathered near the palace gates, some waving republican flags and others watching quietly as police blocked the surrounding roads.

Government officials said an inventory of palace property had been prepared before the handover. The state has also taken control of several palaces, forests and properties formerly used by the royal family, though Gyanendra is expected to retain private assets.

In his remarks, the former king defended his record, saying he had acted in the country’s interest and had never sought confrontation with the people. He said history would judge the monarchy’s role.

Nepal now faces the difficult task of forming a new government, drafting a republican constitution and integrating or rehabilitating thousands of former Maoist combatants. The monarchy’s abolition has removed one of the central disputes of the peace process, but political parties remain divided over power-sharing, federalism and the future structure of the state.

For many Nepalis, Gyanendra’s exit from Narayanhiti closed a turbulent chapter in the country’s history. The palace, once a symbol of royal authority and secrecy, is to reopen as a public institution in a republic still struggling to define itself.

**Kathmandu, Nepal — Former King Gyanendra Says He Will Remain in Nepal as Monarchy Is Abolished After Maoist Election Victory**

Kathmandu — Nepal’s former King Gyanendra has said he has no plans to leave the country, even as the centuries-old monarchy is formally abolished and the Himalayan nation moves toward becoming a republic following a historic election victory by former Maoist rebels.

Speaking amid a dramatic political transition in Kathmandu, Gyanendra made clear that he intends to remain in Nepal as a private citizen. His statement comes after the newly elected Constituent Assembly, dominated by the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist), moved to end the monarchy and reshape the state after years of civil war, street protests and political turmoil.

“I have no intention or plan to leave the country,” Gyanendra said in remarks reported from Kathmandu, seeking to dispel speculation that he might go into exile following the loss of royal power. The former king indicated that he would respect the political changes taking place and continue living in Nepal.

The statement is a significant moment in Nepal’s transformation from a Hindu kingdom ruled by the Shah dynasty into a republic. Gyanendra, who ascended the throne in 2001 after the royal palace massacre that killed King Birendra and much of the royal family, became a deeply polarizing figure after seizing direct power in 2005. His move to dismiss the government and rule by decree triggered mass protests and intensified opposition from political parties, civil society groups and Maoist forces.

The monarchy’s fate was effectively sealed after the Maoists, who fought a decade-long insurgency against the state, emerged as the largest party in elections for the Constituent Assembly. The vote was widely seen as a mandate for sweeping political change, including the abolition of royal rule and the drafting of a new constitution.

In Kathmandu, the political atmosphere remains tense but historic. Crowds have gathered in parts of the capital to celebrate the end of monarchy, waving party flags and chanting republican slogans. Security has been tightened around the former royal palace and key government buildings as authorities seek to prevent unrest during the transition.

The Maoists, led by Pushpa Kamal Dahal, widely known as Prachanda, have pledged to create a “New Nepal” based on republicanism, federalism and social inclusion. Their election success marks a remarkable shift from armed rebellion to mainstream politics. The party has promised to restructure the state, address inequality and bring marginalized communities into political decision-making.

However, major challenges lie ahead. Nepal’s political parties must agree on power-sharing arrangements, the future of the army, the integration or rehabilitation of former Maoist combatants, and the drafting of a new constitution. The country is also facing economic hardship, weak institutions and high public expectations after years of instability.

For royal supporters, Gyanendra’s decision to remain in Nepal may offer reassurance that the transition will not lead to confrontation or exile. For republicans, his statement is being viewed as a symbolic acceptance of the end of royal authority.

The former king’s future residence and status remain sensitive issues. The government has been expected to convert the royal palace into a national museum, underscoring the symbolic transfer of sovereignty from the crown to the people. Gyanendra and his family are expected to vacate the palace as the republic is implemented.

Nepal’s monarchy dated back more than two centuries, with the Shah dynasty playing a central role in unifying and ruling the country. But the institution’s legitimacy eroded sharply after the 2001 palace massacre, Gyanendra’s assumption of power, and his later attempt to rule directly. The 2006 People’s Movement forced him to give up absolute authority and restore parliament, setting the stage for the peace process with the Maoists and the eventual election of the Constituent Assembly.

Now, with the monarchy abolished and Gyanendra declaring that he will stay in Nepal, the country is entering one of the most consequential chapters in its modern history.

The former king’s words suggest a quieter personal role for a man who once held absolute authority. But politically, the moment signals a decisive break with Nepal’s royal past — and the beginning of an uncertain republican future.
